question: What is the primary fluid environment surrounding the body's cells called?
explanation: Extracellular fluid surrounds the body's cells and forms the internal environment that must remain stable for cellular survival. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why is homeostasis called a dynamic state instead of just staying completely still?

options.A: Organs stop functioning entirely when the person is resting quietly
options.B: The body temperature drops significantly every single hour without physical movement
options.C: Internal conditions fluctuate constantly within a normal narrow range around a set point
options.D: Extracellular fluid constantly changes into intracellular fluid to provide energy

explanation: You've got this! Think of homeostasis like riding a bicycle: you're always making small steering adjustments to stay upright, rather than just freezing in place. That's what dynamic means! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h1)

question: Which part of a homeostatic control system detects a change or stimulus in the environment?
explanation: Receptors act as sensors that pick up changes in the environment and forward that data to the control center. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h2)

question: What is the main job of the effector in a homeostatic loop?

options.A: To carry out the final response that alters the internal environment
options.B: To constantly measure the exact temperature of the skin
options.C: To process signals and decide if a change is dangerous
options.D: To store excess glucose until the body needs extra fuel

explanation: Great job! Effectors are the doers—like muscles or sweat glands—that take the instructions and actually fix the imbalance in the body. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h2)

question: Which type of feedback mechanism is most common for maintaining normal daily physiological ranges?
explanation: Negative feedback is the most common control mechanism because it counteracts deviations to keep body systems stable. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h3)

question: When you get a cut, your body triggers blood clotting where each step activates even more clotting. What kind of loop is this?
explanation: Spot on! Positive feedback pushes a process forward until a goal is reached—like forming a solid clot to stop bleeding before it slows down. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h3)

question: What is the medical term when individual cells grow larger in size?
explanation: Think 'hyper' (more/bigger) and 'trophy' (growth). Hypertrophy means the cells are getting bigger, not multiplying! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h4)

question: Why do skeletal muscles get bigger when someone does heavy weightlifting regularly?

options.A: Cellular hypertrophy occurs due to increased functional demand
options.B: Metaplasia transforms fat tissue directly into muscle tissue
options.C: Atrophy removes damaged proteins to make space for fluid
options.D: Hyperplasia creates brand new muscle fibers in the tissue

explanation: You're crushing this! Since muscle fibers don't easily make brand new cells, the existing cells bulk up (hypertrophy) to handle the heavy workload. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h4)

question: What is metaplasia?

options.A: An abnormal decrease in the total number of cells in an organ
options.B: The complete death of tissue due to a lack of oxygen supply
options.C: The replacement of one mature cell type by another mature cell type
options.D: Uncontrolled cell division that forms a malignant tumor mass

explanation: Metaplasia is a reversible adaptation where one adult cell type swaps for another type better suited to handle ongoing stress. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why do nurses and doctors pay very close attention when a lab report mentions dysplasia?

options.A: It guarantees that the tissue has already formed a malignant tumor
options.B: It causes immediate and total loss of function in the affected organ
options.C: It means the cells have permanently shrunk due to prolonged starvation
options.D: It represents disordered cellular growth that can progress to cancer

explanation: Dysplasia means the cells are looking disorganized and weird. Catching this early is key because it can sometimes turn into cancer if the stress doesn't stop. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h5)

question: When you face sudden stress, what is the very first stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome?
explanation: That's right! The alarm reaction is your classic 'fight-or-flight' moment where adrenaline kicks in and gets your body ready for quick action. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h6)

question: What happens to the body during the stage of exhaustion under long-term, chronic stress?

options.A: The parasympathetic system shuts down the brain permanently
options.B: Blood pressure returns to normal and all energy stores double
options.C: Reserves are depleted and organ systems begin to break down
options.D: Cells undergo rapid atrophy to save energy for the heart

explanation: Well done! When stress goes on for way too long, the body runs out of coping energy, leading to exhaustion and a higher risk of getting sick. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h6)

question: How do nurses use the idea of homeostatic imbalance when caring for patients?

options.A: To cure infections without using antibiotics by encouraging the patient to rest
options.B: To reverse genetic mutations that caused cellular metaplasia years ago
options.C: To connect abnormal vital signs and lab results to failing physiological control loops
options.D: To prevent the aging process from slowing down organ system functions

explanation: Spot on! When a patient's vital signs are out of whack, a good nurse sees it as a sign that the body's balancing loops are struggling and need help. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h7)

question: How does normal aging usually affect the body's homeostatic control systems?

options.A: They increase in functional reserve capacity across all organs
options.B: They stop using feedback loops and rely entirely on positive feedback
options.C: They become less efficient at responding to environmental stress
options.D: They speed up and become overly sensitive to minor changes

explanation: You've got it! As people grow older, their internal systems take a bit longer to bounce back from stress like extreme heat, cold, or sudden illness. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h7)
